referenceHardware.runtime: llama.cpp b3500, single thread per token, 8 threads

promptSet.prompt: Explain in two sentences why quantization reduces LLM memory usage.
promptSet.systemPrompt: You are a concise technical writer. Answer in plain English, no markdown.

samples: Quantization stores each weight in fewer bits, so the model file and the tensors held in RAM both shrink in direct proportion. Smaller tensors also move through caches faster, which is why quantized models often run quicker on the same CPU.
Weights are usually 16-bit floats, but most of that precision is unused for inference. Compressing them to 8-bit or 4-bit integers cuts memory by 2x or 4x while keeping outputs nearly identical.
Each layer holds millions of weight numbers. Lowering the precision of those numbers reduces the bytes per weight, so the entire model occupies less RAM and fits onto smaller devices.

Quantization stores each weight in fewer bits, so the model file and the activations held in RAM both shrink in proportion. Smaller tensors also move through CPU caches faster, which usually boosts throughput.
Weights start out as 16-bit floats, but most of that precision is unnecessary at inference time. Converting them to 8-bit integers cuts memory roughly in half and keeps outputs nearly identical.
Every layer holds millions of weight numbers. Lowering the precision of those numbers reduces the bytes per weight, so the whole model occupies less RAM and runs on smaller devices.
Quantization stores each weight in fewer bits, so both the model file and the data held in RAM shrink in proportion. Smaller tensors move through caches faster, which often makes inference quicker.
